```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggplot2)
library(gstat)
load("../data/RainData.RData")   # data.frame `dati` (stations of all years) and `grid`
```

## Question 1

**1.1 Distribution of annual rainfall**

```{r}
#| label: eda-rain
#| fig-height: 4
#| 
annees <- c(1973, 1974, 1980)

op <- par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

for (an in annees) {
  dati_an <- dati |> 
    dplyr::filter(anno == an)
  
  cat("\n=== Année :", an, "===\n")
  print(summary(dati_an$totanno))
  cat("SD:", sd(dati_an$totanno, na.rm = TRUE), 
      "| CV:", sd(dati_an$totanno, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(dati_an$totanno, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
  
  hist(dati_an$totanno, 
       breaks = 20, 
       col = "grey80", 
       main = paste("Histogram -", an), 
       xlab = "Annual rainfall (mm)")
  
  boxplot(dati_an$totanno, 
          main = paste("Boxplot -", an), 
          ylab = "mm")
}

par(op)
```

Comparative Exploratory Analysis of Annual Rainfall (1973, 1974, and 1980): The exploratory analysis of annual rainfall (totanno) across 1973, 1974, and 1980 reveals a consistent positively skewed distribution across all three periods, as evidenced by the right-tailed histograms, elevated upper whiskers, and the systematic presence of high-rainfall outliers (\> 2100 mm). Despite this structural similarity, typically driven by orographic effects at higher-elevation stations, notable inter-annual variations are observed in both central tendency and dispersion. Specifically, 1973 represents the wettest year overall, characterized by the highest median (\~1150–1200 mm) and the broadest interquartile range (\~850–1600 mm), reflecting a high proportion of stations receiving between 1300 mm and 1900 mm. Conversely, 1974 exhibits a marked downward shift toward drier conditions, with the primary frequency peak dropping to 700–800 mm, a lower median (\~1000 mm), and a more compact interquartile spread (\~650–1300 mm). Finally, 1980 displays an intermediate central tendency (median near 1000 mm) but stands out for having the widest overall range (spanning from \~250 mm to nearly 3000 mm), highlighting stronger spatial contrasts between dry lowland stations and extreme wet outliers.

**1.2 Rainfall vs elevation**

```{r}
#| label: eda-rain
#| fig-height: 4

# 1973
ggplot(dati73, aes(Quota, totanno)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Elevation (m)", y = "Annual rainfall (mm)",
       title = "Rainfall vs elevation, 1973")

# correlation measures and tests
ct_p <- cor.test(dati73$Quota, dati73$totanno, method = "pearson")
ct_p

# simple linear model
fit_lm <- lm(totanno ~ Quota, data = dati73)
summary(fit_lm)
confint(fit_lm)

# 1974

ggplot(data_1974, aes(Quota, totanno)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Elevation (m)", y = "Annual rainfall (mm)",
       title = "Rainfall vs elevation, 1974")

# correlation measures and tests
ct_p <- cor.test(data_1974$Quota, data_1974$totanno, method = "pearson")
ct_p

# simple linear model
fit_lm <- lm(totanno ~ Quota, data = data_1974)
summary(fit_lm)
confint(fit_lm)

# 1980

ggplot(data_1980, aes(Quota, totanno)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Elevation (m)", y = "Annual rainfall (mm)",
       title = "Rainfall vs elevation, 1980")

# correlation measures and tests
ct_p <- cor.test(data_1980$Quota, data_1980$totanno, method = "pearson")
ct_p

# simple linear model
fit_lm <- lm(totanno ~ Quota, data = data_1980)
summary(fit_lm)
confint(fit_lm)
```

Across all three analyzed years (1973, 1974, and 1980), the scatter plots and linear regression models consistently demonstrate a positive linear relationship between elevation (Quota) and annual rainfall (totanno). This reflects the classic orographic effect, where precipitation increases as air masses are forced upward by topography, cooling and condensing moisture along the slopes.

```{r}
#| label: lm-diagnostics
#| fig-height: 5

# 1973
fit_lm <- lm(totanno ~ Quota, data = dati73)
summary(fit_lm)

shapiro.test(residuals(fit_lm))

dati73$res_lm <- residuals(fit_lm)
vr <- variogram(res_lm ~ 1, locations = ~ XUTM + YUTM, data = dati73)

set.seed(123)
nsim <- 99
cutoff_val <- max(vr$dist) * 1.0001
width_val <- cutoff_val / nrow(vr)

sim_gamma <- replicate(nsim, {
  dati73$res_perm <- sample(dati73$res_lm)
  vr_perm <- variogram(res_perm ~ 1, locations = ~ XUTM + YUTM, data = dati73, 
                       cutoff = cutoff_val, width = width_val)
  vr_perm$gamma[1:nrow(vr)]
})

env_low <- apply(sim_gamma, 1, min, na.rm = TRUE)
env_high <- apply(sim_gamma, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)

plot(vr$dist, vr$gamma,
     ylim = range(c(vr$gamma, env_low, env_high), na.rm = TRUE),
     pch = 19, col = "black",
     xlab = "Distance", ylab = "Semivariance",
     main = "Semivariogram of the residuals (totanno ~ Quota) with MC Envelope, 1973")
lines(vr$dist, vr$gamma, col = "black", lwd = 1.5)
lines(vr$dist, env_low, lty = 2, col = "red", lwd = 1.5)
lines(vr$dist, env_high, lty = 2, col = "red", lwd = 1.5)


# 1974

shapiro.test(residuals(fit_lm))

lines(vr$dist, vr$gamma, col = "black", lwd = 1.5)

# 1980

summary(fit_lm)

})

env_high <- apply(sim_gamma, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Evaluating the residuals of the linear regression models (totanno \~ Quota) requires a cautious diagnostic interpretation regarding both distributional normality and spatial independence. In 1973, the Shapiro–Wilk test yields a non-significant result ($W = 0.9947, p = 0.7449$); however, failing to reject the null hypothesis only indicates the absence of strong evidence against normality and does not formally confirm that the residuals follow a Gaussian distribution. Conversely, for both 1974 ($W = 0.9615, p = 5.39 \times 10^{-5}$) and 1980 ($W = 0.9615, p = 8.21 \times 10^{-5}$), the Shapiro–Wilk test strongly rejects the normality hypothesis, reflecting pronounced positive skewness and extreme positive residuals exceeding $+1400\text{ mm}$. More importantly, the Shapiro–Wilk test evaluates only the marginal distribution of the residuals and is completely blind to their geographical arrangement; therefore, even a non-significant result like that of 1973 cannot validate the standard Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) assumptions in a spatial context.

Then, over the three-year period, the empirical semivariograms of the residuals fall well below the lower bound of the Monte Carlo permutation envelope at short and medium distances: residual spatial dependence remains significant up to approximately 75 km in 1973, 37 km in 1974, and 33 km in 1980. This positive spatial autocorrelation of the residuals violates the independence assumption of ordinary least squares (OLS), which leads to an underestimation of standard errors and makes the $t$-tests and $p$-values of the classical regression artificially too optimistic.

**1.3 Map of the rainfall**

```{r}
# 1973

ggplot(dati73, aes(XUTM, YUTM, colour = totanno)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "mm") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "XUTM (m)", y = "YUTM (m)", title = "Annual rainfall by station, 1973")

# 1974

ggplot(data_1974, aes(XUTM, YUTM, colour = totanno)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "mm") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "XUTM (m)", y = "YUTM (m)", title = "Annual rainfall by station, 1974")

# 1980

ggplot(data_1980, aes(XUTM, YUTM, colour = totanno)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "mm") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "XUTM (m)", y = "YUTM (m)", title = "Annual rainfall by station, 1980")
```

The spatial distribution of annual rainfall across the monitoring network in 1973, 1974, and 1980 reveals a consistent geographical pattern and strong positive spatial autocorrelation. Across all three periods, the lowest precipitation levels (\< 1000 mm, shown in dark purple) are systematically concentrated in the northern plains, along the eastern border, and at the southern tip, whereas the highest totals (\> 1500 mm, in orange and yellow) align along the central and western mountainous ridge due to the orographic effect. Despite this structural stability, marked inter-annual variations emerge in both the intensity and location of rainfall maxima: 1973 exhibits the most widespread high-precipitation zone with a central peak exceeding 2500 mm (YUTM ≈ 4,370,000 m), whereas 1974 shows an overall drying trend where maximum values (\~2000–2400 mm) retreat toward the northwestern coastal sector (YUTM ≈ 4,460,000 m). Finally, 1980 combines predominantly low-to-moderate peripheral rainfall with sharp local contrasts, featuring a wet cluster in the northwest and an isolated extreme peak approaching 3000 mm in the central massif.

# Question 2: choice of p in the IDW estimator

## Method

The power $p$ of the IDW estimator controls how fast the weight of a station decreases with the distance: with $p$ close to 0 all stations count almost the same and the prediction is close to the overall mean; with a large $p$ only the nearest stations matter and the surface follows the observations closely. For each year (1973, 1974 and 1980), we choose $p$ by leave-one-out cross-validation: each station is removed in turn and predicted from the others, and we keep the $p$ with the smallest RMSE, searching on a grid from 0.25 to 8 and refining around the minimum. The result is compared with a simple reference, the mean of the other stations.

```{r}
#| label: q2-function
#| code-fold: true
loocv_idw <- function(d, p_grid = seq(0.25, 8, by = 0.25)) {
  z  <- d$totanno; n <- length(z)
  Dm <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(d$XUTM, d$YUTM))); diag(Dm) <- Inf   # a station never predicts itself
  pred <- function(p) { W <- Dm^(-p); as.vector(W %*% z) / rowSums(W) }
  rmse <- function(p) sqrt(mean((z - pred(p))^2))
  curve <- data.frame(p = p_grid, RMSE = sapply(p_grid, rmse))
  p0  <- curve$p[which.min(curve$RMSE)]
  opt <- optimize(rmse, c(max(0.01, p0 - 0.25), p0 + 0.25))        # refinement around the minimum
  ref <- sqrt(mean((z - (sum(z) - z) / (n - 1))^2))                 # mean of the other stations
  near <- curve$p[curve$RMSE <= 1.01 * opt$objective]               # p giving an RMSE within 1 % of the best
  pr <- pred(opt$minimum)
  hi <- z > quantile(z, 0.9); lo <- z < quantile(z, 0.1)
  list(curve = curve, p_opt = opt$minimum, rmse = opt$objective, ref = ref,
       mae = mean(abs(z - pr)), n = n, p_low = min(near), p_high = max(near),
       r_small = curve$RMSE[1], r_large = curve$RMSE[nrow(curve)],
       cor = cor(z, pr), bias_hi = mean(pr[hi] - z[hi]), bias_lo = mean(pr[lo] - z[lo]),
       cv = data.frame(obs = z, pred = pr))
}

years <- c(1973, 1974, 1980)
q2 <- lapply(years, function(y) loocv_idw(subset(dati, anno == y)))
names(q2) <- years
get <- function(f) sapply(q2, `[[`, f)
```

## Results

```{r}
#| label: q2-table
q2_tab <- data.frame(
  Year = years,
  Stations = get("n"),
  `Optimal p` = round(get("p_opt"), 2),
  `p within 1 % of the best RMSE` = sapply(q2, function(r) paste0(r$p_low, " - ", r$p_high)),
  RMSE = round(get("rmse")),
  MAE = round(get("mae")),
  `RMSE of the reference` = round(get("ref")),
  `MSE reduction (%)` = round(100 * (1 - get("rmse")^2 / get("ref")^2)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(q2_tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

The table gives, for each year, the number of stations, the optimal $p$, the range of $p$ whose RMSE is less than 1 % above the best one, the cross-validation RMSE and MAE (in mm), the RMSE of the reference and the reduction of the mean squared error obtained with the IDW compared with the reference. The optimal $p$ is `r q2_tab[["Optimal p"]][1]` in 1973, `r q2_tab[["Optimal p"]][2]` in 1974 and `r q2_tab[["Optimal p"]][3]` in 1980. In each year the IDW predicts clearly better than the reference: the RMSE goes from `r q2_tab[["RMSE of the reference"]][1]`, `r q2_tab[["RMSE of the reference"]][2]` and `r q2_tab[["RMSE of the reference"]][3]` mm to `r q2_tab$RMSE[1]`, `r q2_tab$RMSE[2]` and `r q2_tab$RMSE[3]` mm, which is a reduction of the mean squared error of `r min(q2_tab[["MSE reduction (%)"]])` to `r max(q2_tab[["MSE reduction (%)"]])` %.

```{r}
#| label: q2-curves
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.8
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(years, function(y) cbind(q2[[as.character(y)]]$curve, Year = y)))
marks  <- data.frame(Year = years, p_opt = get("p_opt"), ref = get("ref"))
ggplot(curves, aes(p, RMSE)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(data = marks, aes(xintercept = p_opt), colour = "firebrick", linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(data = marks, aes(yintercept = ref), colour = "grey40", linetype = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Year, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "p", y = "Leave-one-out RMSE (mm)",
       title = "Choice of p by leave-one-out cross-validation",
       subtitle = "Dashed red: optimal p. Dotted grey: mean of the other stations") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Figure 1: leave-one-out RMSE as a function of p, one panel per year (each panel has its own vertical scale). The dashed red line is the optimal p and the dotted grey line is the RMSE of the reference.*

**Comment on Figure 1.** In each year the RMSE reaches a clear minimum, at $p$ = `r q2_tab[["Optimal p"]][1]`, `r q2_tab[["Optimal p"]][2]` and `r q2_tab[["Optimal p"]][3]`. The curve is flat around it: the values of $p$ within 1 % of the best RMSE form an interval about 1 unit wide (see the table), so the choice of $p$ is not critical.

```{r}
#| label: q2-obs-pred
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.8
cvs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(years, function(y) cbind(q2[[as.character(y)]]$cv, Year = y)))
ggplot(cvs, aes(pred, obs)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + geom_abline(colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ Year, nrow = 1) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Leave-one-out prediction (mm)", y = "Observed (mm)",
       title = "Cross-validation at the optimal p") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Figure 2: observed rainfall against the leave-one-out prediction at the optimal p. The red line is the line prediction = observation.*

**Comment on Figure 2.** The points are spread around the red line, with a correlation between observation and prediction of `r round(get("cor")[1], 2)` in 1973, `r round(get("cor")[2], 2)` in 1974 and `r round(get("cor")[3], 2)` in 1980. The wettest stations (top 10 % of the observed values) are under-predicted, by `r round(-get("bias_hi")[1])`, `r round(-get("bias_hi")[2])` and `r round(-get("bias_hi")[3])` mm on average, and the driest ones (bottom 10 %) are over-predicted, by `r round(get("bias_lo")[1])`, `r round(get("bias_lo")[2])` and `r round(get("bias_lo")[3])` mm.

The optimal values of $p$ are used in the next question to map the rainfall on the prediction grid.

# Question 3: interpolation and map

```{r}
#| label: q3-maps
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 6
#| column: page
library(patchwork)

interpolation_map <- function(data, p_opt, grid, year) {
  fct_grid <- grid
  fct_grid$pred <- idw(totanno ~ 1, locations = ~ XUTM + YUTM, data = data,
                       newdata = grid, idp = p_opt, debug.level = 0)$var1.pred

  ggplot() +
    geom_point(data = fct_grid, aes(XUTM / 1000, YUTM / 1000, colour = pred), size = 1.5) +
    geom_point(data = data, aes(XUTM / 1000, YUTM / 1000), shape = 4, size = 1) +
    scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "mm") +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(x = "X (km)", y = "Y (km)",
         title = paste0(year, " (p = ", round(p_opt, 2), ")")) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}

interpolation_map(subset(dati, anno == 1973), 3.125, grid, 1973) +
interpolation_map(subset(dati, anno == 1974), 3.45,  grid, 1974) +
interpolation_map(subset(dati, anno == 1980), 2.62,  grid, 1980) +
  plot_annotation(title = "IDW prediction of annual rainfall",
                  subtitle = "Crosses: stations")
```
